content: The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) is a federal advisory committee that provides expert external advice and guidance to the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) regarding the use of vaccines and related agents to control vaccine-preventable diseases in the civilian population of the United States. Recommendations for routine vaccination in children and adolescents are aligned as much as possible with those from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP), and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG). Similarly, recommendations for routine adult vaccination are reviewed and approved by the American College of Physicians (ACP), AAFP, ACOG, and the American College of Nurse-Midwives. The CDC, its planners, and content experts disclose that they have no financial interests or relationships with manufacturers of commercial products, suppliers of commercial services, or commercial supporters. Presentations do not include discussions of unlabeled uses of products or investigational products. The CDC does not accept recommendations or reports that are not evidence-based. Influenza viruses typically circulate widely in the United States annually from late fall through early spring. While most individuals infected with influenza recover without complications, the virus can cause severe illness and death, particularly in individuals aged 65 years or older, children under 2 years of age, and those with medical conditions that increase their risk of complications. Between the 1976-77 and 2005-06 influenza seasons, annual influenza-associated deaths in the U.S. ranged from 3,000 to 49,000. Annual influenza vaccination is the primary method of preventing influenza and its complications. Routine annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all individuals aged 6 months and older who do not have contraindications. No preferential recommendation is made for one influenza vaccine product over another when multiple appropriate options are available. Trivalent influenza vaccines for the 2013-14 season include an A/California/7/2009 (H1N1)-like virus and an H3N2 virus antigenically similar to the cell-propagated prototype virus. Quadrivalent vaccines include an additional influenza B virus strain. The naming conventions for influenza vaccines have evolved. The abbreviation TIV (Trivalent Inactivated Influenza Vaccine) has been replaced with IIV (Inactivated Influenza Vaccine). For the 2013-14 season, IIVs include egg-based and cell culture-based trivalent inactivated influenza vaccines (IIV3) and egg-based quadrivalent inactivated influenza vaccines (IIV4). Recombinant hemagglutinin influenza vaccine (RIV) is available as a trivalent formulation (RIV3), and live-attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) is available as a quadrivalent formulation (LAIV4). RIV3, an egg-free vaccine, is an option for individuals aged 18-49 years with egg allergies of any severity. Influenza A and B viruses cause epidemic human disease. Influenza A viruses are categorized into subtypes based on surface antigens hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA). Since 1977, influenza A (H1N1), influenza A (H3N2), and influenza B viruses have co-circulated globally. Influenza B viruses are divided into two genetic lineages (Yamagata and Victoria) but are not categorized into subtypes. Antigenic drift, resulting from point mutations and recombination during viral replication, leads to the emergence of antigenic variants, necessitating annual vaccine updates. Antigenic shifts, which involve larger genetic changes, can result in new influenza A virus subtypes capable of causing pandemics. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic was caused by a novel influenza A (H1N1) virus antigenically distinct from previously circulating human H1N1 viruses. This virus originated from swine influenza viruses and was antigenically distinct from human influenza A (H1N1) viruses circulating since 1977. Influenza B viruses undergo antigenic drift less rapidly than influenza A viruses, and both lineages of influenza B have co-circulated in recent seasons. Annual influenza epidemics in the U.S. typically occur during fall and winter. Increases in healthcare visits for acute febrile respiratory illness coincide with periods of increased influenza activity. Excess deaths and hospitalizations during influenza seasons have been estimated for decades. From 1979-80 to 2000-01, annual influenza-associated hospitalizations ranged from approximately 55,000 to 431,000, with a mean of 226,000. Estimated annual deaths attributable to influenza ranged from 3,000 to 49,000 between the 1976-77 and 2006-07 seasons. Influenza infection rates are highest among children, but complications, hospitalizations, and deaths are greatest among individuals aged 65 years or older, children under 5 years (especially those under 2 years), and individuals with high-risk medical conditions. Among children under 5 years, influenza is a common cause of outpatient medical visits. Hospitalization rates for children under 5 years with high-risk medical conditions are higher than for healthy children. Since 2004, pediatric deaths associated with laboratory-confirmed influenza have been nationally reportable. During the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, approximately 300 pediatric deaths occurred, most of whom had underlying medical conditions. Hospitalization rates during typical influenza seasons are highest among adults aged 65 years or older. Deaths associated with influenza are also most frequent among older adults, with an estimated annual average of 21,098 influenza-related deaths among adults aged 65 years or older from 1976-77 to 2006-07, accounting for approximately 90% of annual influenza-related deaths across all age groups. Among healthy younger adults, seasonal influenza illness is typically less severe, but influenza remains an important cause of outpatient medical visits and work absenteeism. Pregnant women are at increased risk for severe influenza illness, as observed during the 1918-19, 1957-58, and 2009-10 pandemics. Severe infections among postpartum women were also observed during the 2009-10 pandemic. Case reports and observational studies suggest that pregnancy increases the risk of seasonal influenza complications for the mother. However, infants born to women with laboratory-confirmed influenza during pregnancy do not have higher rates of low birth weight, congenital abnormalities, or lower Apgar scores compared to infants born to uninfected women. The effectiveness of influenza vaccines depends on factors such as the recipient's age and immune status, the similarity between vaccine and circulating virus strains, and the outcome being measured. Randomized controlled trials measuring laboratory-confirmed influenza virus infections provide the most persuasive evidence of vaccine efficacy. Humoral and cell-mediated immune responses to influenza vaccination have been studied in children and adults. Serum antibodies are considered correlates of vaccine-induced protection. While LAIV induces lower levels of serum antibodies compared to IIV, it more effectively induces cellular immune responses. The composition of influenza vaccines is updated annually to provide protection against anticipated circulating viruses. Evidence suggests that protection against antigenically similar viruses extends for at least 6-8 months, particularly in non-elderly populations.
